name: sarn
author: wordplay-agent
description: PRIVATE. Tongue-twister list + keyboard row travel. CLUE: one lowercase letter L followed by 3-6 digits, each 1-9, e.g. 's3142'. SOLUTION: exactly that many whitespace-separated English words (words.is_word, the engine's 235k web2 list), EVERY word starting with L (the kid-visible tongue-twister layer), where word i's ROW TRAVEL equals digit i. Row travel = give each letter its QWERTY row (qwertyuiop=0, asdfghjkl=1, zxcvbnm=2) and sum |row(a)-row(b)| over neighbouring letters, so a top-to-bottom hop counts 2, not 1: 'salt' = 1, 'scrape' = 5, 'crazy' = 6. Case and whitespace are free. INTENDED DISCOVERY PATH: (1) clue = letter + digits and every demo word starts with that letter, so the alliteration clause is free in round 1; (2) the digits are a per-word integer that is NOT length, vowels, consonants, syllables, distinct letters or scrabble score (all measured at 0.0-0.6 %); (3) the leap - type the word and count the row lines your finger crosses; (4) the near miss - counting row CHANGES instead of the distance agrees on 34.9 % of words, i.e. 1.7 % of whole answers versus a 0.07 % floor: a visible 'keyboard, but not quite' gradient that costs one probe cycle to fix. WITNESSES CLOSED (measured, 3000 clues): empty/junk/clue-echo 0.00 %; best constant answer 0.20 %; random words with the right initial and count 0.07 %; one-letter words are impossible because generate never emits a 0 digit and a 1-letter word travels 0; every clue carries >= 2 distinct digits so 'one word repeated' is never valid. The measurement is a TRANSITION count, so the standard no-insight attack 'digit = |word intersect S| for a hidden letter set S' has NO solution: the best greedy subset over 2000 (word,digit) pairs matches 26 % of words and scores 0.75 %, and a least-squares letter-weight model fitted to the ~25 pairs six demos supply fits them 100 % and then scores 0.30 % (2.25 % even with 2000 pairs). Word order matters (travel is unchanged by shuffling a word's letters only 30 % of the time), so no bag-of-letters feature can express it. The alliteration clause also blows the empirically-learnable (word -> number) table up from 9 cells to ~125 while 6 demos supply ~25, killing the table-learning route. GENERATOR: draws real everyday words (proper nouns filtered by an inflection test) from dense (letter, value) cells with >= 5 words each, over 15 letters, so solve always has >= 5 choices per position and demos never repeat; solve prefers words of <= 7 letters so a human can check a demo by hand.
